meta.note: Preview data. All records are Awaiting Evidence Review. Descriptions were drawn from publisher and repository pages retrieved on this date and are not a substitute for the full papers.

items.title: Theories of consciousness
items.read: Abstract as paraphrased on the author's page and an accepted-manuscript record.
items.description: Reviews four approaches: higher-order theories, global workspace theories, re-entry and predictive processing theories, and integrated information theory. For each it covers what the theory aims to explain, its neurobiological commitments, and the evidence offered for it. It then considers how empirical debates might distinguish the theories and outlines three ways theories need to develop for rigorous testing.
items.relevance: Overview used to frame the chamber and to state the open problem of distinguishing theories.
items.limitations: Only the abstract-level description was read for this preview; section-level characterizations of each theory were not read.

items.title: Integrated information theory: from consciousness to its physical substrate
items.read: Bibliographic record only. The abstract was not available during the preview build.
items.description: A review article on integrated information theory, written by proponents of the theory.
items.relevance: Listed as foundational reading for IIT.
items.limitations: Content not read. No claim in this chamber rests on this paper's text.

items.title: Experimental and theoretical approaches to conscious processing
items.read: Review text retrieved as a PDF and summarized.
items.description: Reviews how information becomes consciously accessible (reportable subjective experience), drawing on neuroimaging and neurophysiology studies that minimally contrast conscious and nonconscious processing, and compares these findings with theoretical models, especially the global neuronal workspace. It concludes that conscious access is marked by late amplification of relevant sensory activity, long-distance cortico-cortical synchronization at beta and gamma frequencies, and ignition of a large-scale prefronto-parietal network. It presents the global neuronal workspace as a cortical alternative to Baars's global workspace.
items.relevance: Core review of the empirical signatures that GNWT associates with conscious access.
items.limitations: Authored by the theory's main proponents. The final page range was not confirmed.

items.title: Conscious processing and the global neuronal workspace hypothesis
items.read: Open-access full text retrieved and summarized.
items.description: Reviews the tenets and neuroanatomy of the global neuronal workspace hypothesis. It proposes that conscious states involve a non-linear 'ignition' tied to recurrent processing that amplifies and sustains a representation so that many processors can access it. It examines the hypothesis against data on conscious versus nonconscious content and states, especially general anesthesia, and discusses attention and working memory. It lists predictions and acknowledges unresolved issues, such as the interpretation of late components like the P3.
items.relevance: Main current statement of GNWT's mechanisms, predictions, and acknowledged limitations.
items.limitations: Authored by proponents. The review itself notes that most evidence is correlational and that findings from animal models may not transfer directly to humans.

items.title: A neuronal model of a global workspace in effortful cognitive tasks
items.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
items.description: Proposes two computational spaces: specialized modular processors, and a global workspace of distributed, densely interconnected neurons with long-range axons recruited mainly when specialized processors cannot handle a task alone. A computer simulation of the Stroop task shows workspace activity rising during learning, effortful performance, and after errors. The authors link the model to dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and anterior cingulate.
items.relevance: An early formal neuronal model from which the global neuronal workspace line of work developed.
items.limitations: A computational model of an effortful task, not a test of consciousness.

items.title: An information integration theory of consciousness
items.description: Proposes a theory of what consciousness is and how it might be measured, drawing on two features of experience, its large repertoire of possible states (differentiation) and the unity of each experience (integration). It links the amount of consciousness to a quantity, Φ, describing how much causally effective information a set of elements can integrate, and argues that the theory fits findings such as the importance of the thalamocortical system and the reduction of consciousness in dreamless sleep. It states that the theory implies consciousness is fundamental, graded, and could in principle be built into artificial systems.
items.relevance: Early statement of integrated information theory.
items.limitations: A single-author theoretical proposal. Its fit with neurobiological findings is the author's argument.

items.title: Integrated information theory (IIT) 4.0: Formulating the properties of phenomenal existence in physical terms
items.read: Open-access full text retrieved and summarized.
items.description: Presents the current formulation of IIT. It lists a zeroth axiom (experience exists) and five essential properties of experience: intrinsicality, information, integration, exclusion, and composition. Each is translated into a postulate about the physical substrate, which must have cause-effect power, act within itself, select a specific cause-effect state, form an irreducible whole, be bounded by a maximal set of units, and specify a structured cause-effect profile. The paper states that these conditions are necessary and sufficient for consciousness, that IIT yields testable predictions (some already tested), and that the formalism is still a work in progress.
items.relevance: Main current statement of IIT's central proposition and mechanisms.
items.limitations: Authored by proponents. The authors state that the formal examples use small simulated networks, that the completeness of the axioms rests on introspection and reasoning, and that alternative candidate properties are conceivable.

items.title: An adversarial collaboration protocol for testing contrasting predictions of global neuronal workspace and integrated information theory
items.read: Open-access text retrieved and summarized; the last portion of the page was not read.
items.description: Describes a preregistered adversarial collaboration between proponents of GNWT and IIT, with experiments testing contrasting predictions about where and when neural correlates of visual consciousness occur, using fMRI, M-EEG, and intracranial EEG across independent labs. It states contrasting predictions on the location of the correlates, decoding of conscious content, temporal dynamics, pre-stimulus activity, and functional connectivity.
items.relevance: The source for the specific contrasting predictions shown in the GNWT versus IIT comparison.
items.limitations: A protocol: it states the predictions and design, not the results. Predictions are those agreed by the proponents for this test and may not exhaust each theory's commitments.

items.title: Adversarial testing of global neuronal workspace and integrated information theories of consciousness
authors: et al. (42 names are listed on the publisher record)
items.read: Publisher record, as retrieved through an institutional repository page.
items.description: Reports an open-science adversarial collaboration testing IIT against GNWT, with 256 human participants and fMRI, MEG, and intracranial EEG. The authors report results that partly align with predictions of both theories while substantially challenging key claims of each: no sustained posterior synchronization, which they say contradicts the claim that network connectivity specifies consciousness, and a general lack of ignition at stimulus offset with limited prefrontal representation of certain conscious dimensions. They argue for a quantitative framework for systematic theory testing.
items.relevance: Direct comparative test of the two theories' predictions.
items.limitations: Only the abstract-level description was read. The test covers specific predictions in one experimental setting (the published Experiment 1); the project page says a second experiment was still underway. The paper does not declare either theory proven or disproven.

items.title: The unfolding argument: Why IIT and other causal structure theories cannot explain consciousness
items.read: Record and abstract closing sentence retrieved from an institutional repository.
items.description: Argues that theories that tie consciousness to causal structure, naming integrated information theory and recurrent processing theory, face a problem, using theorems from the theory of computation. Its stated conclusion is that causal structure theories are either false or outside the realm of science.
items.relevance: A published philosophical and formal objection to IIT and RPT.
items.limitations: A theoretical argument. Proponents dispute its premises; the full argument and responses were not read for this preview.

items.title: Empirical support for higher-order theories of conscious awareness
items.read: A repository summary of the paper.
items.description: Argues that conscious awareness depends on higher-order representations, which are mental states that represent oneself as being in a particular state. It compares the view with first-order, global workspace, and recurrent visual processing theories, focusing on evidence that tells them apart. It responds to objections, including that prefrontal activity reflects attention rather than awareness and that prefrontal lesions do not eliminate awareness, and concludes that the higher-order approach, though rooted in philosophy, is empirically testable and has received substantial support.
items.relevance: Primary advocacy review for higher-order theories.
items.limitations: Written by proponents. Only a short summary was read, so specific predictions and evidence were not extracted.

items.title: Towards a true neural stance on consciousness
items.read: Bibliographic record only. The abstract was not available during the preview build.
items.description: A 2006 article by Victor Lamme, whose work is associated with recurrent processing theory.
items.relevance: Listed as a primary reference for RPT.
items.limitations: Content not read. The description of RPT in this chamber comes from a secondary web entry and needs review against this paper.

items.title: Lamme's Recurrent Processing Theory (Landscape of Consciousness)
items.description: A web entry describing Lamme's recurrent processing theory: consciousness arises when sensory areas engage in recurrent (feedback) processing, located at the third of four described stages of visual processing. It notes criticisms by Ned Block and a contrast with global workspace theory. The page relies largely on secondary sources (a Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy entry and Block's 2023 book) rather than Lamme's papers directly.
items.relevance: Used only as a pointer to the theory's outline until primary sources are reviewed.
items.limitations: Secondary and unsigned. Not a substitute for the primary literature. Publication date not stated.

items.title: The attention schema theory: a mechanistic account of subjective awareness
items.description: Proposes that subjective awareness is the brain's simplified internal model of its own attention, analogous to a body schema. It argues this explains how awareness and attention can dissociate and how people can be aware of internal and external events, states testable predictions, and reviews literature that it describes as supporting some of them. The authors acknowledge disputed points, such as the top-down versus bottom-up distinction and whether awareness can occur without attention, and describe the evidence as suggestive.
items.relevance: Primary statement of attention schema theory.
items.limitations: Authored by the theory's proponents; the review of supporting studies is theirs and was not independently checked.

items.title: Predictive processing as a systematic basis for identifying the neural correlates of consciousness
items.description: Argues that the search for neural correlates of consciousness needs a principled foundation, and proposes the predictive processing framework for brain function as a candidate. The authors stress that predictive processing is not, at the outset, a theory of consciousness, and present that as an advantage.
items.relevance: Shows how predictive processing is positioned relative to consciousness science, without treating it as a single accepted theory.
items.limitations: A philosophical argument. Page numbers were not shown on the retrieved page.

items.title: Consciousness in Artificial Intelligence: Insights from the Science of Consciousness
items.read: arXiv abstract page retrieved and paraphrased.
items.description: Argues for studying AI consciousness empirically by assessing existing AI systems against leading neuroscientific theories. It reviews recurrent processing, global workspace, higher-order, predictive processing, and attention schema theories, derives computational indicator properties, and evaluates several recent AI systems against them. It concludes that no current AI systems appear to be conscious, and that there are no obvious barriers to building conscious AI systems.
items.relevance: Shows how several of these theories have been used to frame questions about artificial systems.
items.limitations: A preprint; no journal version was mentioned on the page. Its indicator properties depend on the theories it draws from. Integrated information theory is not among the theories named in the abstract.

items.title: Prominent Consciousness Theory Is Slammed as Bogus Science (news report on an open letter)
items.read: News article retrieved and summarized. The letter itself was not read.
items.description: Reports that a letter signed by 124 scholars was posted to the PsyArXiv preprint server in September 2023 arguing that integrated information theory should be labelled pseudoscience, citing among other points that some core assumptions are untestable and a gap between IIT's standing and its media attention. It also reports disagreement, including researchers who say IIT makes testable predictions and that one prediction was tested.
items.relevance: Documents a public dispute about IIT's scientific status, with responses.
items.limitations: A secondary news report, not the letter. The term 'pseudoscience' was left undefined according to the report. Treat as evidence that a dispute exists, not as a finding.
